No Tax on Overtime in 2026: How the Deduction Really Works

No tax on overtime is a federal deduction for 2025–2028, not an exemption. See what qualifies, the $12,500/$25,000 caps, and how to claim it on your return.

"No tax on overtime" sounds like overtime pay just became tax-free. It did not. The 2025 law created a federal income-tax deduction for the overtime premium only — claimed when you file your return, capped per year, and temporary through 2028. Your paychecks still show withholding, your state taxes are mostly unchanged, and the full 1.5× overtime rate was never on the table.

As the technical tools architect at Hourly Wage Converter, I see the same confusion every tax season: workers expecting bigger paychecks, then frustration when nothing changes. This guide explains exactly what the deduction covers, walks through the math with real numbers, and shows how to claim it — so you get the benefit you are actually owed and stop expecting one you are not.

No Tax on Overtime: The Quick Answer

Here is the entire law in five points:

  • It is a deduction, not an exemption. You still owe tax on overtime during the year; you deduct part of it when you file.
  • Only the premium qualifies. On time-and-a-half pay, just the extra "half" is deductible — the base hourly rate for those hours is fully taxable.
  • Annual caps apply: $12,500 for single filers, $25,000 for joint filers.
  • Temporary: tax years 2025 through 2028 only.
  • Federal income tax only. Payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare) and most state income taxes still apply to the full amount.

If you remember nothing else: half the premium, capped, at filing time, federal only.

A Deduction, Not an Exemption: What the Law Actually Does

The phrase "no tax on overtime" is political shorthand, and it misleads. An exemption would mean overtime income never enters your taxable income at all — no withholding, no reporting, no tax. That is not what happened.

What Congress created is an above-the-line deduction: when you file your federal return, you subtract your qualified overtime premium (up to the cap) from your income before calculating tax. Consequences that surprise people:

  • Withholding is unchanged. Your employer keeps withholding federal income tax from overtime exactly as before.
  • You claim it once a year, on your return — reported on a separate schedule attached to Form 1040.
  • No itemizing required. Above-the-line means it works whether you take the standard deduction or itemize.
  • It reduces income tax only — not Social Security or Medicare tax, which are withheld on the full overtime amount all year.

Think of it this way: the government did not stop taxing your overtime. It gave you a coupon, redeemable once a year, for part of the tax — and only on the premium half.

What Counts: Only the Overtime Premium Qualifies

This is the single most misunderstood part of the law. "Qualified overtime compensation" means only the extra amount paid above your regular rate — the premium — not your total overtime earnings.

Pay Component ($20/hr base, 5 OT hours) Amount Deductible?
Regular rate for the 5 hours ($20 × 5) $100.00 No — fully taxable
Overtime premium, the extra half ($10 × 5) $50.00 Yes — up to annual cap
Total overtime pay received ($30 × 5) $150.00 Only the $50 premium portion

A worker earning $150 in overtime pay in a week can deduct at most $50 of it. Anyone telling you the whole $150 is tax-free is wrong — and that misunderstanding is the source of most disappointment at tax time.

The premium must also be required by the Fair Labor Standards Act — the federal half-time premium for hours over 40 in a workweek. Voluntary extra pay your employer offers above the legal requirement (for example, double-time on holidays where not legally required) generally does not count as qualified overtime compensation.

The $12,500 / $25,000 Annual Caps Explained

Even the qualifying premium is capped per tax year:

  • Single filers: up to $12,500 of overtime premium per year
  • Joint filers: up to $25,000 per year

To put that in perspective: at a $10/hour premium, you would need 1,250 overtime hours in a year to hit the single-filer cap — roughly 24 overtime hours every single week. Most workers will never approach the cap, which means for typical overtime earners the practical limit is simply however much premium they actually earned.

There is also an income phaseout: the deduction begins to shrink above certain income thresholds. Because the exact thresholds are subject to IRS guidance, treat any specific number you see online with caution and check the current instructions for the tax year you are filing.

Why Your Paycheck Still Shows Tax Withholding

The number-one complaint since the law passed: "My paycheck didn't change." Here is why that is exactly what the law designed:

  • Employers were not told to change withholding. Payroll systems still withhold federal income tax from overtime using the normal rules.
  • Overtime is often withheld at a flat 22% federal supplemental rate, which may be higher or lower than your actual marginal rate — that mismatch already existed before this law.
  • The benefit arrives at filing. When you claim the deduction, your taxable income drops, which either shrinks what you owe or grows your refund.

So the correct expectation is not a bigger paycheck in July — it is a smaller tax bill (or bigger refund) next April. If you want the benefit sooner, you could adjust your W-4 withholding to account for the expected deduction, but that requires estimating your annual overtime premium in advance. Most workers are better off letting it land at filing time.

Tax benefit ≈ deductible premium × your marginal tax rate

Example: $3,000 of qualifying premium × 22% marginal rate = about $660 less federal income tax. The premium itself was still subject to Social Security, Medicare, and (usually) state tax.

W-2 Reporting: The New Separate Overtime Line

Starting with 2026 W-2s, employers must separately report qualified overtime compensation — breaking out the premium from your total wages. This is the paper trail the IRS uses to verify your deduction.

What this means for you:

  • Check your W-2 carefully. The separately stated overtime amount is the starting point for your deduction — keep your own records too, in case of discrepancies.
  • Keep pay stubs. If your employer's reporting is wrong or incomplete, your stubs are your evidence of the premium you earned.
  • Tax software will ask for it. Expect a specific input for qualified overtime when you file; do not lump it in with general wages.

Who Qualifies and Who Does Not

Situation Qualifies?
Hourly non-exempt worker paid time-and-a-half over 40 hrs/week Yes — the classic case
Salaried non-exempt worker receiving FLSA overtime premium Yes — if the premium is FLSA-required
Holiday or weekend premium pay not required by the FLSA Generally no — voluntary premiums do not count
Exempt salaried employee with no overtime pay at all No — nothing to deduct
Self-employed / gig worker "overtime" No — no employer-paid FLSA premium exists
Comp time taken instead of overtime pay No — no premium was paid

What About State Income Taxes?

For most workers, the answer is disappointing but simple: your state still taxes the full overtime amount. The deduction exists only in the federal tax code, and most states have not adopted a matching provision.

A few practical notes:

  • States with no income tax (Texas, Florida, Washington, and others) are unaffected either way — there was no state tax on the overtime to begin with.
  • In states with income tax, assume the premium remains fully taxable unless your state has explicitly conformed — verify before filing rather than assuming.
  • State conformity can change year to year, so recheck each filing season instead of relying on last year's answer.

How to Claim the Deduction at Tax Time

The mechanics are straightforward, but each step matters:

  • 1. Gather your W-2. Find the separately reported qualified overtime compensation figure.
  • 2. Cross-check with pay stubs. Confirm the premium total matches your records; flag discrepancies with your employer early.
  • 3. Apply the cap. Use the smaller of your actual premium and the $12,500 / $25,000 cap.
  • 4. Enter it on the designated schedule. Follow your tax software's prompts or your preparer's guidance — it goes on a separate schedule with Form 1040, not buried in wages.
  • 5. Keep records. Retain W-2s and pay stubs for at least three years in case of IRS questions.

Because this is general education rather than personal tax advice: if your situation involves large overtime amounts, multiple employers, or amended returns for 2025, a tax professional can confirm you are claiming the right figure.

Common Misconceptions to Avoid

  • "My whole overtime check is tax-free now." Only the premium half qualifies — roughly a third of a time-and-a-half check.
  • "My employer should stop withholding." Withholding rules did not change; the deduction happens at filing.
  • "It covers Social Security and Medicare too." FICA taxes apply to the full overtime amount, premium included.
  • "My state follows the federal rule automatically." Most states do not conform — check yours.
  • "This is permanent." The provision covers 2025–2028. Plan as if it ends unless Congress acts.
  • "I need to itemize." It is above-the-line; standard-deduction filers qualify.

Frequently Asked Questions About No Tax on Overtime

Direct answers to the questions workers ask most about the overtime deduction:

Is overtime taxed at a higher rate than regular pay?

No. Overtime is taxed at your normal marginal income-tax rate — the same rate as the rest of your earnings. It can feel higher because overtime pushes more income into a higher bracket and because employers often withhold at a flat supplemental rate (currently 22% federal) that may exceed your actual rate. The 2025–2028 overtime deduction does not change your withholding; it reduces taxable income when you file. See also: Is Overtime Taxed at a Higher Rate? (2026).

Is all of my overtime pay tax-free under the new law?

No. Only the overtime premium — the extra half of time-and-a-half pay — qualifies for the deduction. If you earn $20/hour and work overtime at $30/hour, only the $10/hour premium portion is deductible, not the full $30. Your regular $20/hour base for those hours remains fully taxable.

When did no tax on overtime start, and how long does it last?

The deduction applies to tax years 2025 through 2028. It is a temporary provision, not a permanent change to the tax code. Unless Congress extends it, overtime premiums become fully taxable again starting with tax year 2029.

Do I have to itemize deductions to claim it?

No. The overtime deduction is an above-the-line deduction, meaning you can claim it whether you take the standard deduction or itemize. It is reported on a separate schedule with your federal return.

Why didn’t my paycheck get bigger after the law passed?

Because the law created an income-tax deduction claimed at filing time, not a change to payroll withholding. Your employer still withholds federal income tax from overtime pay as before. The tax benefit shows up as a smaller tax bill or larger refund when you file your return — not as a bigger paycheck.

Does no tax on overtime apply to state income taxes?

Generally no. Most states have not conformed to the federal deduction, so overtime premiums remain taxable at the state level in most places. A few states may conform in future years, so verify your state’s current rules before filing.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

The overtime deduction is real money — but only if you understand its boundaries. Here is your action plan:

No Tax on Overtime: Summary Checklist

  • Know what qualifies: Only the FLSA-required premium (the extra half of time-and-a-half) — not your full overtime check.
  • Track the caps: $12,500 single / $25,000 joint per year; the deduction covers 2025–2028.
  • Expect it at filing, not payday: Withholding is unchanged — the benefit lands on your tax return.
  • Verify your W-2: Starting with 2026, qualified overtime is reported separately — cross-check it against your pay stubs.
  • Model your gross first: Use the overtime calculator below to see your earnings, then estimate the deduction from the premium.

Calculation Methodology & Sources

Overtime pay examples in this guide use the federal Fair Labor Standards Act baseline: time-and-a-half (1.5×) the regular hourly rate for hours over 40 per workweek. The deduction figures ($12,500 single / $25,000 joint caps; tax years 2025–2028; premium-only qualification) reflect the federal provision as enacted; thresholds and IRS guidance can change, so verify against current IRS instructions before filing.
